strengths: The paper identifies an important and underexplored evaluation gap: precise language-conditioned recognition, editing, and reconstruction of molecular structures, rather than ambiguous molecule-caption or downstream property-prediction tasks.

MolLangBench covers complementary tasks and representations. The 18 recognition subtasks span topology, functional groups, substructures, and stereochemistry, while editing and generation test increasingly demanding structure-language interactions.

The core editing and generation sets use a notably careful curation procedure involving independent annotation, peer refinement, reconstruction by two validators, and exact structural matching. This provides meaningful evidence for annotation quality.

The evaluation includes numerous contemporary general-purpose, reasoning, vision-language, image-generation, and chemistry-specific models. Per-task results, validity versus exact-match accuracy, model snapshots, repeated-run variance for o3, and several prompt-sensitivity checks are useful.

The findings are practically informative: substantial gaps remain in atom localization, stereochemical reasoning, exact editing, and especially reconstruction from detailed descriptions. The paper is generally clear and contains extensive examples and supplementary results.
weaknesses: The baseline suite does not include tool-augmented language models, RDKit-backed agents, or strong modular chemistry systems. Many recognition tasks are exactly solvable by standard cheminformatics after parsing the input, so evaluating only unaided LLMs weakens the broad conclusion that current AI systems lack these capabilities. Likewise, editing and generation lack competitive specialized text-to-molecule or graph-based baselines.

There is no measured human baseline, despite repeated claims that tasks are trivial or simple for humans and that descriptions are reconstructible by someone with basic organic-chemistry training. Atom enumeration, stereochemistry, and long descriptions can themselves induce human error; validator acceptance does not establish typical human accuracy or task difficulty.

The editing and generation core sets contain only 200 examples each. Confidence intervals and significance tests are not reported, and GPT-5 is evaluated only once. Consequently, several model differences and the claim that GPT-5 wins 19 of 20 tasks may not be statistically meaningful.

Important evaluation details are underspecified, including decoding parameters, precise normalization/canonicalization rules, treatment of salts, charges, tautomers and stereoisomers, exact-match metric implementation, failure parsing, and manual-evaluation adjudication. The OCR analysis is based on very few positive images and does not strongly validate automated image scoring.

Dataset construction lacks sufficient analysis of duplicates, overlap among task splits, molecule overlap with public model pretraining data, structural diversity, label distributions, and difficulty. Sampling merely 'tries' to balance labels, while the extended sets use a weaker protocol and markedly different edit-category distributions, making core-versus-extended comparisons difficult to interpret.

The proposed explanation that BPE tokenization causes localization errors is speculative and supported by one anecdotal example rather than controlled tokenization or representation experiments. Similarly, monotonic improvement with model release date is circularly presented as evidence of benchmark quality.

The benchmark is framed as reflecting realistic chemical workflows, but most recognition questions are synthetic graph queries and generation descriptions are highly engineered structural specifications. The paper does not demonstrate that benchmark performance predicts success on practical molecular-design or laboratory tasks.

Reproducibility depends heavily on proprietary, changing APIs and manual annotations. Although model snapshots are listed, the manuscript does not provide a complete reproducibility package within the paper, and the displayed dataset/code references are unresolved. Data licensing, annotator qualifications or agreement statistics, and compensation or ethics details are also absent.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant gap: precise language-conditioned molecular recognition, editing, and reconstruction are important capabilities that conventional chemistry benchmarks do not fully test.
The benchmark covers complementary representations and tasks, including topology, functional groups, stereochemistry, molecule editing, and description-to-structure generation.
The core editing and generation data use a thoughtful multi-stage process involving independent reconstruction by chemistry-trained validators.

The experiments include numerous recent general-purpose and chemistry-specific models, model snapshots, exact-match and validity metrics, repeated-run variance for o3, and some prompt-sensitivity analysis.
weaknesses: There are serious internal inconsistencies that undermine confidence in the reported results. GPT Image 1 editing performance is variously reported as 13.5% in the abstract, 8% accuracy with 51% validity in Table 2 and the main text, and a single 13.5% value in Table S7 despite its caption claiming validity/accuracy pairs. The generation entries are likewise formatted inconsistently.

At least one showcased benchmark example appears substantively corrupted: in Figure S5(c), the textual description specifies an indole-like system with chlorine substituents and a formyl group, while the displayed ground-truth structure visibly contains a different heterocyclic/amide architecture and fluorine atoms. Such a conspicuous mismatch directly challenges the central claim of meticulously validated, unambiguous annotations.

Reproducibility is inadequate from the manuscript alone. Complete prompts, decoding parameters, reasoning-effort settings, output parsing rules, canonicalization procedures, and treatment of stereochemistry, salts, tautomers, and equivalent SMILES are not specified sufficiently. Dataset and code links also appear incomplete in the submitted document.

The evaluation sets for editing and generation are small—only 200 core examples each—and several important edit categories contain extremely few cases, such as one tautomerization, two charge edits, and three relocation edits. Aggregate accuracy therefore provides weak evidence of broad capability.

The benchmark construction lacks systematic audits of inter-annotator agreement, residual annotation error, scaffold duplication, UniChem source composition, memorization or contamination, and overlap across task sets. Validation by two people is useful but is not a substitute for reporting measured quality statistics.

Several interpretations overreach the evidence. Claims that tasks are trivial for humans are unsupported by a human baseline, the assertion that model ranking validates annotation quality is circular, and the proposed BPE-tokenization explanation is speculative and supported mainly by an anecdotal example.

The image-versus-SMILES comparison is confounded because the interfaces differ: image prompts expose atom indices and highlights, whereas SMILES models must perform enumeration. Image generation is also evaluated through manual or imperfect OCR procedures rather than the same output channel, preventing clean modality conclusions.

The recognition task selection and balancing procedure is underspecified: the authors merely state that they “try” to balance labels and select difficult cases. Exact class distributions are absent, making statements such as performance being below random guessing difficult to verify.

The related-work positioning is too sweeping. The claim that existing molecule-language datasets are not structure-grounded is not established through a careful comparison of task coverage, evaluation protocols, or contemporary molecular instruction benchmarks.

Overall, the benchmark idea is promising, but the visible annotation mismatch, contradictory headline numbers, underspecified evaluation, and limited dataset validation are major issues rather than minor presentation defects. These problems keep the submission below the standard of a top-tier conference.

strengths: MolLangBench targets an important and under-evaluated capability: precise language-conditioned molecular recognition, editing, and reconstruction, rather than only downstream property or reaction prediction.

The benchmark design emphasizes deterministic answers and exact structural grounding. Recognition labels are generated with cheminformatics tools, while editing and generation examples undergo expert annotation, peer review, and independent reconstruction-based validation.
The task suite is broad and chemically meaningful, covering topology, functional groups, atom localization, stereochemistry, diverse structural edits, and detailed molecule generation.

The empirical study evaluates a wide range of contemporary language and vision-language models. Exact-match results expose substantial weaknesses, especially for stereochemistry, atom localization, and de novo reconstruction.

The appendix adds useful robustness evidence, including repeated-run variance, SMILES enumeration, linguistic paraphrases, chemical-terminology variations, model snapshots, category-level editing results, and analysis of image-based evaluation.
The paper is well organized, visually clear, and likely to provide a useful diagnostic resource for research at the molecule-language interface.
weaknesses: The baseline suite is incomplete for the paper's broad claims about current AI systems. It primarily tests unaided general-purpose models; tool-augmented LLMs, RDKit-enabled agents, retrieval or programmatic baselines, and capable molecular graph models could behave very differently. Chemistry-specific models are evaluated only on editing and appear heavily penalized by instruction-formatting failures.

There are notable reporting inconsistencies. Table 1 reports GPT-5 recognition/localization averages of 92.3%/86.2%, but the abstract and main text call 86.2% the recognition accuracy. Likewise, GPT Image 1 editing accuracy is described as 13.5% in the abstract but as 8.0% under manual evaluation in the main table; the distinction between OCR-derived and manual figures is not presented clearly.

The human-curated core editing and generation sets contain only 200 examples each. The paper provides limited evidence about molecular diversity, near-duplicate control, overlap with model training data, annotation rejection rates, and coverage of rare edit types; several categories contain only one to three examples.

Exact-match accuracy is appropriate for deterministic tasks but gives little insight into near-correct generations, error severity, or chemical similarity. A structured error taxonomy and complementary scaffold, stereochemical, or graph-edit metrics would make the conclusions more informative.

Some causal interpretations are insufficiently supported. Performance increasing with model recency does not itself validate benchmark quality, and the claim that atom-index errors arise from BPE tokenization is based mainly on an illustrative example rather than controlled tokenization experiments.

Reproducibility is limited by dependence on proprietary, changing APIs and a commercial OCR system. Although snapshots and an o3 variance study are supplied, complete decoding configurations, cost estimates, and repeated-run results for the leading GPT-5 baseline are absent.

The manuscript advertises compatibility with graph representations but does not actually evaluate that modality. Claims about a comprehensive molecule-language interface benchmark should therefore be qualified until graph-language evaluation is demonstrated.
The paper does not meaningfully discuss dataset licensing, annotator compensation, or potential misuse considerations associated with molecule-generation benchmarks.

strengths: Introduces a clear and useful benchmark spanning three fundamental molecule–language capabilities: structural recognition, instruction-based editing, and generation from detailed descriptions.

The benchmark construction is unusually careful. Recognition labels are generated programmatically with RDKit, while the core editing and generation sets use peer review plus independent reconstruction by two chemistry-trained validators.

Evaluation is broad, covering numerous frontier and open models, chemistry-specific language models, graph–language systems, image inputs, SELFIES, and image generation. Exact-match accuracy, validity, localization accuracy, and structural similarity expose complementary failure modes.
The recognition suite contains diverse, precisely specified tasks and generally requires localization in addition to coarse classification, reducing the value of superficial pattern matching.
The paper includes useful robustness and diagnostic analyses, including repeated runs, pass@k, SMILES enumeration, linguistic paraphrases, category-level results, and manual error analysis.
Results reveal concrete and consequential weaknesses—especially stereochemistry, atom enumeration, topology, and de novo construction—and the dataset and code are stated to be released.
weaknesses: The experimental setup is not documented sufficiently for strong reproducibility: full prompts, decoding parameters, reasoning-effort settings, output parsing rules, API configurations, and exact definitions of canonical exact match and Tanimoto similarity are not clearly specified in the manuscript.

There is no measured human baseline, despite repeated claims that the tasks are simple or trivial for humans. Human accuracy, completion time, and inter-annotator agreement on a held-out sample would help establish task validity and the claimed human–model gap.

The evaluated systems are predominantly unaided zero-shot models. Missing rule-based, tool-using, or agentic baselines—such as LLMs allowed to invoke RDKit—limit the broad claim that current AI systems cannot perform these tasks and make it difficult to separate language–molecule alignment failures from SMILES bookkeeping failures.

Sampling and balancing procedures for recognition tasks are underspecified. Exact label distributions, selection algorithms, duplicate and near-duplicate handling, molecule standardization, and overlap among tasks or with the auxiliary dataset should be reported.

The editing and generation test sets contain only 200 core examples each, with highly uneven edit-category counts. Several categories have only one to three examples, making category-level conclusions unreliable; uncertainty intervals are also absent from most model comparisons.

The claim that the curated molecules are representative of UniChem is not established by a qualitative 2D t-SNE plot. Quantitative diversity, scaffold overlap, and distributional comparisons are needed.

The downstream property-prediction experiment does not establish a causal relationship between recognition ability and prediction performance. It omits sample sizes, split details, class balance, stronger metrics, and significance testing, while structure-first prompting also grants additional computation and changes the prompt substantially.

Several interpretations are stronger than the evidence: monotonic performance across newer models does not validate annotation quality, and the attribution of localization errors to BPE tokenization is speculative and supported only by an anecdotal example.

Presentation contains inconsistencies or ambiguities, including references to 20 recognition tasks despite the primary suite listing 18, and inconsistent or incomplete reporting of GPT Image 1 validity in the tables. These should be resolved before publication.

strengths: Introduces a potentially useful structure-grounded benchmark spanning recognition, language-directed editing, and description-to-structure generation across SMILES, image, and preliminary graph-language settings.
The core editing and generation sets employ careful curation: peer refinement, independent reconstruction by two validators, exact structure comparison, and rejection of unresolved examples.
Evaluation covers numerous frontier, open, and chemistry-specific models, supplemented by prompt perturbations, repeated trials, pass@k results, SELFIES experiments, and qualitative error analysis.

Programmatic RDKit labels and atom-localization requirements make the recognition tasks more diagnostic than simple classification. weaknesses: Benchmark validity is not established through blinded human baselines, despite claims that the tasks are intuitive or solvable with basic chemistry knowledge. Validator agreement does not quantify human accuracy, ambiguity, or completion time on the final test prompts.

The evaluation omits crucial practical baselines such as tool-augmented LLMs using RDKit, constrained molecular decoding, and strong task-specific editing or generation systems. Many recognition tasks are exactly solvable with standard cheminformatics tools, limiting the significance of standalone zero-shot LLM comparisons.

Results are internally inconsistent: the benchmark defines 18 recognition tasks but states that GPT-5 wins 19 of 20; GPT Image 1 editing performance appears as 13.5% in the introduction, 8% in Table 2 and Appendix A.17, and 0.135 in Table S5. Table S5 also provides only one image-model number despite specifying three metrics.

Editing and generation contain only 200 core examples each, while the additional sets use a weaker validation process. Confidence intervals and paired significance tests are absent for most model comparisons, so some reported margins may reflect sampling noise.

Reproducibility details are incomplete, including balancing rules, duplicate or scaffold overlap, structure-equivalence and canonicalization procedures, Tanimoto fingerprint settings, treatment of salts and tautomers, decoding parameters, and complete task prompts.
A 2D t-SNE plot does not demonstrate that the manually curated, size-filtered molecules are representative of UniChem. The diversity and representativeness claims are therefore overstated.

Several conclusions are insufficiently supported. The tokenization explanation rests largely on an anecdote, while the downstream property experiment confounds structural analysis with additional reasoning and does not establish a causal relationship between recognition accuracy and prediction.

The scope is narrower than the title suggests: recognition centers on basic graph queries and common motifs, while editing and generation do not capture property-driven design, reactions, synthesis constraints, or broader chemistry workflows.
Annotator count, expertise, compensation, independence, and relevant dataset licensing considerations are not adequately documented.

strengths: MolLangBench addresses an important and under-evaluated prerequisite for AI-assisted chemistry by jointly covering molecular recognition, language-guided editing, and description-to-structure generation.

The core editing and generation sets are curated with a strong protocol involving peer refinement and independent reconstruction by two validators, with useful validation and rejection statistics reported.
Evaluation is broad, spanning frontier general and reasoning models, chemistry-specific LLMs, graph-language models, vision-language models, and image generation systems.

Exact structural matching and atom-level localization provide substantially more rigorous evaluation than loose caption-similarity metrics. The error analysis identifies meaningful deficiencies in stereochemistry, topology, substituent placement, and molecular syntax.
The appendix contains valuable robustness experiments, including repeated runs, pass@k, prompt paraphrases, SMILES enumeration, SELFIES inputs, complex substructures, and OCR-versus-human evaluation.

The benchmark is likely to be a useful resource for the molecule-language community, and the main empirical conclusion—that current models remain unreliable at precise molecular manipulation—is well supported.
weaknesses: The editing and generation core sets contain only 200 examples each. This limits coverage of the very large chemical and instruction spaces, while no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for the primary model comparisons.

Claims that the curated molecules are representative of broader UniChem space rely largely on a qualitative 2D t-SNE visualization. The sampling and balancing procedures, deduplication controls, and overlap among benchmark and auxiliary sets are insufficiently specified.

Several headline numbers are inconsistent or mislabeled. The abstract describes GPT-5's 86.2% result as recognition accuracy, whereas Table 1 reports 92.3% recognition and 86.2% localization. GPT Image 1 editing performance is variously described as 13.5% and 8%, while the relevant tables report incompatible formats.

Some tasks, particularly SMILES atom enumeration and exact output formatting, conflate chemical understanding with string parsing and bookkeeping. The image experiments only partly resolve this, and practically relevant tool-augmented LLM baselines using RDKit are absent.

The assertion that these tasks are simple for humans is not supported by a controlled human baseline. Validator reconstruction establishes annotation quality but does not quantify human task accuracy or difficulty under the model evaluation protocol.

The downstream property-prediction experiment does not establish that recognition ability causes improved predictions: asking for a structural description also adds reasoning tokens and changes the prompting strategy. Dataset splits, evaluation sample sizes, and stronger controls are not reported.

Reproducibility details for commercial-model inference are incomplete beyond model snapshots: decoding parameters, exact prompts for every task, API settings, and complete output-processing rules are not fully documented in the manuscript. Dataset licensing and annotator compensation are also not discussed.
